Kouxian is the Chinese general term for the jaw harp, a plucked idiophone within the idiophones, with the Hornbostel–Sachs number 121.2. It is built as a bamboo or metal tongue fixed at one end to a frame; the player holds the frame against the lips, sets the tongue vibrating with a finger or by pulling a cord attached to the frame, and changes the shape of the mouth to resonate it. It is common among the non-Han peoples of southwest China such as Yunnan, Guangxi and Guizhou and also appears among the indigenous peoples of Taiwan; it can be used for one's own amusement, for courtship between men and women, to accompany song and dance, or in ensemble with other instruments. Several pieces can be bound into a fan, and modern sets of three or more can be tuned to the first few notes of a pentatonic scale.
口弦的音色清脆而獨特，帶有明亮的金屬質感，卻又不失溫潤的民族風韻。其音域較窄，主: The kouxian's timbre is bright and distinctive, with a luminous metallic quality that still keeps a warm, folk-like character. Its range is narrow and lies mainly in the upper middle register; its volume is relatively small but it carries well. Its way of resonating is highly distinctive: the player holds the instrument close to the lips and uses the mouth as a resonating chamber, changing the shape of the mouth and the position of the tongue to alter timbre and pitch. This mechanism gives the timbre subtle variation and a rich set of overtones. Compared with the pipa, the kouxian is cleaner and finer; compared with the dizi it has more of a cold metallic edge. Its sound sits between an instrument and the voice, highly expressive and intimate, often with a slight nasal resonance.
口簧琴的起源有亞洲與西伯利亞阿爾泰山脈兩說；已知最古老實物可追溯至公元前4000: The origin of the jaw harp is argued either for Asia or for the Altai mountains of Siberia; the oldest known specimens go back to Neolithic sites of 4000 BC. In China it was called huang from before the Qin, had such names as bamboo huang and iron huang in the Tang and Song, was mostly called kouqin in the Ming and Qing and is now generally called kouxian, and it is widespread among the non-Han peoples of Yunnan, Guangxi and Guizhou. Almost every indigenous people of Taiwan uses it except the Tao, and it is especially prominent among the Atayal, Truku and Sediq. In 1943 Kurosawa Takatomo classified it by playing method into the plucked jaw harp and the cord jaw harp; in 2015 the Truku Lahan Losing introduced 3D printing and laser cutting, lowering the barrier to making one.

演奏時以左手執持首部，將簧框橫置於口前，以雙唇輕含琴臺；右手可撥動股部或舌尖，或: To play, the left hand holds the head, the frame is held across the mouth and the table is taken lightly between the lips; the right hand plucks the shank or the tip of the tongue, or pulls a thin cord tied to the shank, setting the tongue vibrating. The mouth then acts as the resonator, and by changing the size of the mouth the player brings out natural overtones. A beginner can work through four steps — hold the frame, take it into the mouth, pluck the tongue, shape the mouth — and then try the pitch combinations of multi-piece kouxian sets.
